source_batch.unit_label: Module C unit 9 (courseware unit 25): the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016, corporate insolvency resolution, resolution plans, liquidation and the pre-packaged process

facts.statement: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) consolidates the laws on reorganisation and insolvency resolution into one Code, so viable businesses no longer face a maze of laws. Insolvency is a situation where an individual's or entity's liabilities exceed its assets and it cannot pay its debts; bankruptcy is the legal recognition of insolvency beyond resolution, where a court adjudges the person bankrupt and a trustee sells property and discharges obligations. Part II applies to companies and limited liability partnerships (corporate debtors), personal guarantors to corporate debtors and any other body incorporated under law that the Central Government notifies; Part III applies to partnership and proprietorship concerns and individuals. The ecosystem comprises the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) as regulator of insolvency professionals, insolvency professional agencies, insolvency professional entities and information utilities (and the authority for registered valuers); insolvency professionals (interim resolution professional, resolution professional, liquidator, bankruptcy trustee) licensed by IBBI; information utilities, which are reservoirs of financial information with a certificate of default; financial creditors (who have lent money for time value) and operational creditors (who supplied goods or services on credit or paid advances for them); the committee of creditors; the corporate debtor; and the judiciary: the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and its appellate tribunal NCLAT for corporate debtors, the Debt Recovery Tribunal and DRAT for non-corporate debtors, and the Supreme Court.

The Code shifted the law from "debtors in possession" to "creditors in control": on appointment of the interim resolution professional, who takes over as CEO of the corporate debtor, the powers of the board of directors are suspended, and on formation of the committee of creditors it supersedes the board. The original promoters or their related parties are barred from bidding for resolution of the corporate entity in default (section 29A), which takes ownership, control and management away from the existing promoters. The courseware describes the Code as debtor-friendly in that it views default from the perspective of chances of reviving the business, distinguishing the business from its promoters.

The Code applies to the insolvency and liquidation of corporate debtors where the minimum amount of default is Rs 1 lakh; the Central Government may notify a higher minimum of not more than Rs 1 crore (the courseware says the figure is Rs 1 crore). A financial creditor, by itself or jointly with other financial creditors, may apply to the Adjudicating Authority to start a corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP) when a default has occurred; the courseware adds that an operational creditor or the corporate debtor itself may also apply, and that default means non-payment of dues in full or in part to any creditor, so the process can be started by a third party for dues owed to it even when the accounts with banks are standard. In the 2026 amendment of section 7 the Adjudicating Authority admits or rejects a financial creditor's application within 14 days, after giving notice to rectify defects within 7 days. On the insolvency commencement date the Adjudicating Authority declares a moratorium prohibiting: suits or continuation of suits and proceedings against the corporate debtor including execution of any judgement or decree; transferring, encumbering, alienating or disposing of its assets; any action to foreclose, recover or enforce security interest, including under the SARFAESI Act; and recovery of property by an owner or lessor from the corporate debtor. Supply of essential goods or services is not terminated during the moratorium, and goods or services critical to preserve the corporate debtor as a going concern are protected on the resolution professional's view. The proposing applicant names an insolvency professional for appointment as interim resolution professional (IRP); on appointment the IRP takes over all powers of the board and management, and runs the corporate debtor as a going concern; if the operational creditor does not propose one, the NCLT appoints an IRP after consulting IBBI within 14 days.
facts.locator: IBC_2016_CONSOLIDATED_2021 sections 4, 7(1) and 14; IBC_AMENDMENT_ACT_2026 section 4; S01 printed p. 534

facts.statement: The corporate insolvency resolution process must be completed within 180 days from the date of admission of the application. If the committee of creditors resolves by a vote of 66 per cent of the voting shares, the resolution professional files an application to the Adjudicating Authority for an extension beyond 180 days; the Authority may extend by a period it thinks fit, not exceeding 90 days, and an extension is granted not more than once. The process must in any case be completed within 330 days from the insolvency commencement date, including any extension and the time taken in legal proceedings. Under the 2026 section 12A, the Adjudicating Authority may allow withdrawal of an application admitted under section 7, 9 or 10 on an application by the resolution professional with the approval of 90 per cent of the voting share of the committee of creditors; withdrawal is not allowed before the committee of creditors is constituted and not after the first invitation for resolution plans is issued; the Authority decides within 30 days of receipt.

After collating claims and determining the corporate debtor's financial position, the interim resolution professional constitutes a committee of creditors (CoC), which comprises all the financial creditors of the corporate debtor; a financial creditor that is a related party of the corporate debtor has no right of representation, participation or voting in the committee (with an exception for a financial sector regulated creditor that is a related party only because of conversion of debt into equity before the insolvency commencement date). Where debts are owed to several financial creditors as part of a consortium, each is part of the committee with its voting share based on the financial debt owed to it; where a person is both a financial and operational creditor, it is a financial creditor to the extent of the financial debt and is included with voting share proportionate to it; where the terms provide for a single trustee or agent for a consortium or syndicated facility, each financial creditor may authorise the agent, represent itself, appoint an insolvency professional or vote jointly with others. The first meeting of the committee is held within seven days of its constitution. By a majority vote of not less than 66 per cent of the voting share of the financial creditors the committee either appoints the interim resolution professional as the resolution professional or replaces the interim resolution professional with another. A vote of 66 per cent of the voting share is also required to approve a resolution plan, to extend the process beyond 180 days and to decide to liquidate the corporate debtor; withdrawal needs 90 per cent. The courseware adds that the committee includes representation of the operational creditors with a limited role (a non-voting observer role, except where there are no financial creditors), and describes the quorum as 33 per cent by value and the routine decision threshold as 51 per cent.
facts.locator: IBC_2016_CONSOLIDATED_2021 sections 21, 22(1)-(2), 30(4), 33(2), 12(2); S01 printed pp. 533 and 537 (courseware statements marked in the text)

facts.statement: The courseware gives a model CIRP timeline (from IBBI regulations amended up to 4 July 2025), with T the date of commencement: public announcement inviting claims within 3 days of appointment of the IRP (T+3), claims submitted for 14 days from appointment (T+14), constitution of the CoC after verification (T+23), first meeting of the CoC within 7 days of the report certifying constitution (T+30) with the resolution on the resolution professional, the IRP performing the functions of the RP till appointment (T+40), appointment of valuers within 7 days of the RP's appointment and not later than the 47th day (T+47), the RP's opinion on preferential and other transactions by day 75 and determination by day 115, applications for appropriate relief by day 130, the information memorandum within 95 days (T+95), Form G and invitation for expression of interest within 60 days (T+60), submission of expressions of interest at least 15 days later (T+75), provisional list of resolution applicants within 10 days (T+85), objections within 5 days (T+90), final list within 10 days (T+100), request for resolution plans within 5 days of the final list (T+105), receipt of plans at least 30 days later (T+135), submission of the CoC approved plan to the Adjudicating Authority (T+165) and approval by the Authority within 180 days (T=180). The information memorandum compiles information on the corporate debtor including assets and liabilities at commencement, financial statements for the last two years, list of creditors and claims, related party debts, guarantees and workforce; the evaluation matrix sets the criteria to evaluate plans; the resolution valuers (two registered valuers) estimate the fair value and liquidation value, the liquidation value being the average of the two closest estimates where there are differences.
facts.locator: S01 printed pp. 534-538 and 545 (regulations not retrieved)

facts.statement: A person is not eligible to submit a resolution plan under section 29A if the person, or any other person acting jointly or in concert with them: (a) is an undischarged insolvent; (b) is a wilful defaulter in accordance with the RBI guidelines; (c) at the time of submission of the plan has an account, or an account of a corporate debtor under their management or control or of which they are a promoter, classified as a non-performing asset and at least one year has lapsed from the classification to the commencement of the CIRP (unless the person pays all overdue amounts with interest and charges before submission of the plan; the clause does not apply to a financial entity that is not a related party of the corporate debtor); (d) has been convicted of an offence punishable with imprisonment for two years or more under an Act specified in the Twelfth Schedule or for seven years or more under any law (the bar ends two years after release); (e) is disqualified to act as a director under the Companies Act, 2013; (f) is prohibited by SEBI from trading in securities or accessing the securities markets; (g) has been a promoter or in the management or control of a corporate debtor in which a preferential, undervalued, extortionate credit or fraudulent transaction has taken place and in respect of which an order has been made by the Adjudicating Authority; and (h) has executed a guarantee in favour of a creditor in respect of a corporate debtor against which a CIRP is pending or in respect of whom a guarantee has been invoked and remains unpaid; the section also bars persons with ineligibility under laws of another country and persons connected to ineligible persons, and the courseware lists these ten grounds.

A resolution applicant submits a resolution plan to the resolution professional with an affidavit that it is eligible under section 29A. The courseware describes the plan as an action plan for insolvency resolution that must state the amount payable to operational creditors and financial creditors, how the interests of all stakeholders are dealt with, past failures of the applicant or related parties, the term and implementation schedule and management during the term, how the cause of default is addressed, that it is technically and financially feasible and viable, the approvals needed and a statement of the applicant's experience and capacity; it must provide for payment of insolvency resolution costs and, to operational creditors, an amount not less than the liquidation value, in priority to financial creditors. The resolution professional examines each plan for compliance and places it before the committee of creditors, which evaluates the plans strictly on the evaluation matrix and may approve a plan by a vote of not less than 66 per cent of the voting share of the financial creditors, after considering feasibility and viability, the manner of distribution (which may take account of the priority in section 53 and the priority and value of security interest) and other requirements. The approved plan goes to the Adjudicating Authority for approval. The applicant may attend CoC meetings as an observer.
facts.locator: IBC_2016_CONSOLIDATED_2021 section 30(1) and 30(4); S01 printed p. 539 (the contents of a plan as the courseware states them; section 30(2) was amended by the 2026 Act and is marked needs_review)

facts.statement: Liquidation starts when: the Adjudicating Authority does not receive a resolution plan before the expiry of the insolvency resolution process period or the maximum period permitted under section 12; or it rejects the resolution plan for non-compliance with the requirements; or, at any time before confirmation of a plan (and even before the information memorandum is prepared), the resolution professional intimates the decision of the committee of creditors, approved by not less than 66 per cent of the voting share, to liquidate; or the corporate debtor contravenes an approved resolution plan and an affected person applies. The Adjudicating Authority passes an order requiring the corporate debtor to be liquidated, issues a public announcement that it is in liquidation and sends the order to the authority with which the corporate debtor is registered. The courseware says the resolution professional can be appointed liquidator unless ineligible, that the liquidator announces appointment in newspapers and invites claims within 5 days, and describes the liquidator's steps (stakeholders' list within 45 days of the last date for claims, a stakeholders' consultation committee within 60 days, an asset memorandum and a preliminary report within 75 days of liquidation commencement, progress reports each quarter, liquidation within one year with a sale period allowing an extra 90 days, final report and an application for dissolution). On the Adjudicating Authority's dissolution order the corporate debtor ceases to exist and a copy of the order goes to the registrar within seven days.
facts.locator: IBC_2016_CONSOLIDATED_2021 sections 33 and 54; S01 printed pp. 539-548 (regulation-level steps from the courseware, needs_review)

facts.statement: In liquidation the proceeds from the sale of the liquidation assets are distributed in this order, notwithstanding any other law: (a) the insolvency resolution process costs and the liquidation costs, paid in full; (b) ranking equally, workmen's dues for the 24 months preceding the liquidation commencement date and debts owed to a secured creditor who has relinquished its security; (c) wages and unpaid dues owed to employees other than workmen for the 12 months preceding the liquidation commencement date; (d) financial debts owed to unsecured creditors; (e) ranking equally, amounts due to the Central and State Governments for the two years preceding the liquidation commencement date and debts owed to a secured creditor for any amount unpaid following enforcement of its security interest; (f) any remaining debts and dues; (g) preference shareholders, if any; and (h) equity shareholders or partners. Within a class of equal ranking, each debt is paid in full or in equal proportion if the proceeds are insufficient; contractual arrangements that disrupt the order are disregarded; the liquidator's fees are deducted proportionately from each class. By the 2026 explanation, where the value of the security interest relinquished is less than the debt owed to the secured creditor, that creditor is a secured creditor to the extent of the value of the security and an unsecured creditor for the rest. A secured creditor may opt to stay outside the liquidation and enforce its security itself; if it relinquishes the security to the liquidator it is in clause (b); if it enforces and the proceeds fall short, the unpaid balance ranks in clause (e); any surplus from enforcement must be tendered to the liquidator.
facts.locator: IBC_2016_CONSOLIDATED_2021 section 53; IBC_AMENDMENT_ACT_2026 section 32; S01 printed pp. 546-547

facts.statement: The pre-packaged insolvency resolution process (PIRP) is available for corporate debtors classified as micro, small or medium enterprises, and for a corporate debtor that commits a default referred to in section 4, subject to conditions. The corporate debtor must not have completed a PIRP or CIRP during the three years preceding the initiation date, must not be undergoing a CIRP or be under a liquidation order, and must be eligible under section 29A. Financial creditors who are not related parties, representing not less than 66 per cent in value of the financial debt due to such creditors, approve the proposal for the name of the insolvency professional to act as resolution professional and approve the filing of the application (with the base resolution plan placed before them); a majority of directors or partners make a declaration (including that the application will be filed within a definite period not exceeding 90 days and that the process is not to defraud any person); and the members pass a special resolution (or at least three-fourths of the partners pass a resolution) approving the filing. The Adjudicating Authority admits or rejects the application within 14 days (with seven days to rectify defects). The PIRP must be completed within 120 days from the pre-packaged insolvency commencement date, and the resolution professional submits the plan approved by the committee of creditors to the Adjudicating Authority within 90 days. The courseware describes PIRP as a debtor-in-possession model (the corporate debtor submits a base resolution plan and stays in management with the creditors in control only on failure), compared with CIRP in which the creditors control the debtor from the start, and that PIRP terminates if the plan is not approved in time, with a three-year cool-off and moratorium from commencement.
facts.locator: IBC_2016_CONSOLIDATED_2021 sections 54A to 54D; S01 printed pp. 549-550

payload.title: The Code, who it covers and who runs it
payload.core_explanation_md:
**IBC 2016** puts the laws on reorganisation and insolvency into **one Code**.

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Insolvency** | **Liabilities exceed assets**; cannot pay debts |
| **Bankruptcy** | **Legal recognition** of insolvency **beyond resolution**; a **trustee** sells property and discharges obligations |

| Part | Applies to |
| --- | --- |
| **Part II** | **Companies and LLPs** (**corporate debtors**), **personal guarantors** to them, and other bodies the Government notifies |
| **Part III** | **Partnership and proprietorship concerns** and **individuals** |

**The ecosystem**

- **IBBI:** the **regulator** (of **insolvency professionals, agencies, entities and information utilities**).
- **Insolvency professionals:** **IRP, RP, liquidator, bankruptcy trustee**.
- **Information utilities:** hold **financial information** and the **certificate of default**.
- **Financial creditors:** **lent money** (time value). **Operational creditors:** supplied **goods or services on credit**, or took **advances** for them.
- **Committee of creditors (CoC).**
- **Courts:** **NCLT** and **NCLAT** (corporate), **DRT** and **DRAT** (individuals and partnerships), **Supreme Court**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware stresses that the Code is a consolidation, which is why it is called a Code rather than an Act.

self_check.prompt_text: Which tribunal is the adjudicating authority for corporate debtors?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), with NCLAT for appeals.

payload.title: From debtors in possession to creditors in control
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Before the Code:** the **debtor stayed in possession** and the creditor chased it through many laws.

**Under the Code:**

1. On **appointment of the IRP**, the **board's powers are suspended** and the IRP takes over as **CEO**.
2. When the **committee of creditors** is formed, it **supersedes the board**.
3. **Original promoters and their related parties** cannot bid for the **corporate debtor** (**section 29A**): ownership, control and management leave the existing promoters.

The courseware calls the Code **debtor-friendly** in one sense: it asks whether the **business can be revived**, treating the **business separately from its promoters**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The pre-pack reverses part of this: the debtor stays in management while a base plan is prepared.

self_check.prompt_text: What happens to the powers of the board of directors when the IRP is appointed?
self_check.expected_takeaway: They are suspended and the IRP takes over the management.

payload.title: Starting a corporate insolvency resolution process and the moratorium
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Threshold:** the Code applies where the **minimum default is Rs 1 lakh**; the Government may notify a **higher minimum, not above Rs 1 crore** (the courseware gives **Rs 1 crore**).

**Who can apply:** a **financial creditor** (alone or jointly), and, per the courseware, an **operational creditor** or the **corporate debtor**. **Default** means non-payment of **dues in full or part to any creditor**: a third party can start the process even when the bank's account is **standard**.

**Admission:** the Adjudicating Authority admits or rejects a financial creditor's application **within 14 days**, after giving **7 days** to correct defects (2026 amendment).

**Moratorium from the insolvency commencement date prohibits**

1. **Suits and execution** of judgments against the corporate debtor.
2. The corporate debtor **transferring, encumbering or disposing** of assets.
3. **Enforcing security interest**, including under the **SARFAESI Act**.
4. **Recovery of property** by an **owner or lessor**.

**Protected:** supply of **essential goods and services**, and supplies the **RP** treats as **critical** to run the business as a **going concern**.

**IRP:** named by the applicant; **takes over management** and runs the corporate debtor as a **going concern**; for an **operational creditor** application with no proposed IRP, the NCLT appoints one after **consulting IBBI within 14 days**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The moratorium protects assets while the plan is formed; it is why SARFAESI and DRT actions stop.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two actions barred by the moratorium.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Any two of: suits and execution of judgments, disposal of assets by the corporate debtor, enforcement of security interest including SARFAESI action, recovery of property by an owner or lessor.

payload.title: The time limit for the process and withdrawal
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Rule | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| **Basic period** | **180 days** from the **date of admission** of the application |
| **Extension** | The **RP** applies if the **CoC resolves with 66 per cent** of the voting share; the Authority may extend by up to **90 days**, and **only once** |
| **Overall maximum** | **330 days** from the insolvency commencement date, **including any extension** and the **time in legal proceedings** |

**Withdrawal (section 12A as substituted in 2026)**

- The **RP** applies to the Adjudicating Authority with the approval of **90 per cent** of the CoC voting share.
- **Not before** the **CoC is constituted**, and **not after the first invitation** for resolution plans.
- The Authority decides **within 30 days** of receiving the application.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The 330-day cap includes the time spent in litigation, so appeals cannot extend it.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the overall maximum duration of a CIRP including extension and legal proceedings?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 330 days from the insolvency commencement date.

payload.title: Voting shares in the committee of creditors and CIRP timing

The CIRP is admitted on day 1. Find the voting shares in the committee of creditors, whether Banks A and B together can approve a resolution plan, and the latest day by which the process must end if the Authority grants the single permitted extension.

worked_steps.description: The related party has no vote, so it is excluded from the voting total.
Bank A voting share.
Bank B voting share.
Banks A and B together against the 66 per cent needed.
worked_steps.intermediate_result: 77.78 per cent, so the plan can be approved

worked_steps.description: Basic period plus the one permitted extension of up to 90 days.
But the overall cap, including extension and legal proceedings, is 330 days from commencement.
worked_steps.formula_or_substitution: min(270, 330) for the process itself; legal time counts within 330

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Voting shares: A 44.44 per cent, B 33.33 per cent, C 22.22 per cent; A and B together hold 77.78 per cent and can approve the plan; the process runs 180 days, extendable once by up to 90 days, with an absolute cap of 330 days

self_check.prompt_text: What share would Banks A and B hold if Company D were not a related party?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 70 per cent of the Rs 1,000 crore total (400 + 300), still above 66 per cent.

payload.title: The committee of creditors: who is in it and how it votes
payload.core_explanation_md:
After **collating claims**, the IRP forms the **committee of creditors (CoC)** of **all financial creditors**.

- A **related party** financial creditor has **no right of representation, participation or voting** (narrow exception for a **regulated** financial creditor that is related **only by debt-to-equity conversion** before commencement).
- **Consortium:** each financial creditor sits with **voting share by the debt owed to it**; with a single **trustee or agent**, each may **authorise the agent, represent itself, appoint an IP, or vote jointly**.
- A **dual creditor** is a financial creditor for its **financial debt** and an operational creditor for its **operational debt**.
- **First meeting** within **7 days** of constitution.

| Decision | Vote of voting share |
| --- | --- |
| Appoint or replace the **resolution professional** | **66 per cent** |
| **Extend** the process beyond 180 days | **66 per cent** |
| **Approve a resolution plan** | **66 per cent** |
| **Decide to liquidate** | **66 per cent** |
| **Withdraw** the application | **90 per cent** |

**Courseware (needs_review):** operational creditors take an **observer** role (voting only where there are **no financial creditors**); **quorum 33 per cent by value**; routine matters **51 per cent**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Because votes are by value of financial debt, large lenders such as banks dominate decisions.

self_check.prompt_text: What vote is needed to approve a resolution plan?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Not less than 66 per cent of the voting share of the financial creditors.

| Day | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **T+3** | **Public announcement** inviting claims |
| **T+14** | **Claims** submitted (14 days from the IRP's appointment) |
| **T+23** | **CoC constituted** |
| **T+30** | **First CoC meeting**: RP decided |
| **T+40** | IRP performs the RP's functions until an RP is appointed |
| **T+47** | **Valuers** appointed |
| **T+60** | **Form G** and **invitation for expressions of interest** |
| **T+75** | **Expressions of interest** received |
| **T+95** | **Information memorandum** |
| **T+105** | **Request for resolution plans** |
| **T+135** | **Resolution plans** received |
| **T+165** | **CoC approved plan** to the Adjudicating Authority |
| **T=180** | **Approval** by the Authority |

**Documents:** the **information memorandum** (assets and liabilities, **two years' financial statements**, creditors and claims, related party debts, guarantees, workforce) and the **evaluation matrix** (criteria for plans). **Two registered valuers** estimate **fair value and liquidation value**; the **liquidation value** is the **average of the two closest estimates** where there are differences.

payload.title: Who cannot submit a resolution plan: section 29A
payload.core_explanation_md:
A person (or anyone **acting jointly or in concert** with them) **cannot submit a plan** if they:

| | Ground |
| --- | --- |
| (a) | Are an **undischarged insolvent** |
| (b) | Are a **wilful defaulter** (RBI guidelines) |
| (c) | Have an **NPA account** (own, or of a corporate debtor they manage or control or promote) for **at least one year** before the CIRP began, **unless all overdue amounts with interest and charges are paid before submitting the plan**; **does not apply** to a **financial entity** that is **not a related party** of the corporate debtor |
| (d) | Were **convicted**: **2 years or more** under a **Twelfth Schedule** Act, or **7 years or more** under any law (bar ends **two years after release**) |
| (e) | Are **disqualified as a director** under the Companies Act, 2013 |
| (f) | Are **prohibited by SEBI** from the securities market |
| (g) | Were promoter or in control of a corporate debtor in which a **preferential, undervalued, extortionate or fraudulent transaction** occurred and an order was made |
| (h) | Gave a **guarantee** for a corporate debtor against whom a CIRP is pending or whose **invoked guarantee remains unpaid** |

The section also bars those **ineligible under the laws of another country** and **connected persons** of ineligible persons.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: This is the provision that keeps the old promoters from simply buying back the company.

self_check.prompt_text: May a wilful defaulter submit a resolution plan?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: section 29A(b) bars a wilful defaulter.

payload.title: The resolution plan and its approval
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **resolution applicant** submits the plan to the **RP** with an **affidavit of eligibility under section 29A**.

**What the plan states (courseware, needs_review):** amounts to **operational and financial creditors**; treatment of **all stakeholders**; **past failures** of the applicant; **term, schedule and management**; how the **cause of default** is addressed; **feasibility and viability**; **approvals** needed; the applicant's **experience and capacity**. It must provide for **insolvency resolution costs** and pay **operational creditors not less than the liquidation value**, ahead of financial creditors.

**Approval**

1. The **RP checks** each plan for compliance.
2. The **CoC** evaluates the plans strictly on the **evaluation matrix**.
3. A plan is approved by **not less than 66 per cent** of the financial creditors' voting share, considering **feasibility and viability**, the **manner of distribution** (which may reflect the **section 53 priority** and the **value of security**).
4. The approved plan goes to the **Adjudicating Authority**.

The applicant may attend CoC meetings as an **observer**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Section 30(2) on plan contents was amended by the 2026 Act, so the list of contents here is the courseware's account.

self_check.prompt_text: What minimum payment does the courseware say a plan must make to operational creditors?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Not less than the liquidation value.

payload.title: When liquidation starts and how it ends
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The 2026 amendment also lets the Authority declare a moratorium during liquidation and appoint the liquidator in the same order.

self_check.prompt_text: By what vote can the CoC decide to liquidate the corporate debtor?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Not less than 66 per cent of the voting share.

payload.title: The order of priority in liquidation
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Rank | Dues paid |
| --- | --- |
| **(a)** | **Insolvency resolution process costs** and **liquidation costs**, in full |
| **(b)** | **Workmen's dues (24 months)** and **debts to a secured creditor who relinquished security** (rank **equally**) |
| **(c)** | **Wages and dues of other employees (12 months)** |
| **(d)** | **Financial debts owed to unsecured creditors** |
| **(e)** | **Dues to Central and State Governments (2 years)** and **secured creditor's unpaid balance after enforcement** (rank **equally**) |
| **(f)** | **Any remaining debts and dues** |
| **(g)** | **Preference shareholders** |
| **(h)** | **Equity shareholders or partners** |

**Rules:** within a rank, **pay in full or pro rata**; **contracts that disturb the order are ignored**; the **liquidator's fee** is deducted **proportionately from each class**.

**Secured creditor's choice**

- **Relinquish** the security to the liquidator and join at rank (b).
- **Stay outside** and enforce the security itself; any **shortfall** ranks at **(e)**; any **surplus** goes to the liquidator.
- **2026 clarification:** if the security relinquished is worth **less than the debt**, the creditor is **secured to the value of the security** and **unsecured for the rest**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The relinquishing secured creditor shares rank (b) with workmen, which is why many banks weigh the choice.

self_check.prompt_text: Where does a secured creditor who enforces its security and falls short rank for the unpaid balance?
self_check.expected_takeaway: At rank (e), equally with Government dues for two years.

payload.title: Distribution of liquidation proceeds
payload.core_explanation_md: Liquidation proceeds are Rs 60 crore. payload.title: The pre-packaged insolvency resolution process (PIRP)
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Who can use it:** corporate debtors that are **MSMEs**, and other corporate debtors with a section 4 default, subject to conditions.

**Conditions**

- **No PIRP or CIRP in the last three years**; not now in CIRP; no liquidation order; **eligible under section 29A**.
- **Unrelated financial creditors with at least 66 per cent in value** approve **the proposed RP** and the **filing**; the **base resolution plan** is put before them.
- A **majority of directors or partners** declare the filing will be made **within 90 days**, that the process is **not to defraud**, and name the RP.
- **Members pass a special resolution** (or **three-fourths of partners** a resolution) to file.

**Process**

| Step | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Admission | Authority admits or rejects **within 14 days** (7 days to rectify) |
| Whole process | **120 days** from the pre-packaged insolvency commencement date |
| Plan submission | CoC-approved plan to the Authority **within 90 days** |

**Contrast with CIRP (courseware):** PIRP keeps the **debtor in management** with a **base plan** prepared in advance; CIRP puts **creditors in control** from admission; CIRP runs **180 days (extendable to 330)**, PIRP **120 days with no extension**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware's "default up to Rs 1 crore" for PIRP misreads section 4, which only caps the minimum default the Government may notify.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Within 120 days of the pre-packaged insolvency commencement date.

items.title: The Code, who it covers and who runs it
items.core_explanation_md:
**IBC 2016** puts the laws on reorganisation and insolvency into **one Code**.

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Insolvency** | **Liabilities exceed assets**; cannot pay debts |
| **Bankruptcy** | **Legal recognition** of insolvency **beyond resolution**; a **trustee** sells property and discharges obligations |

| Part | Applies to |
| --- | --- |
| **Part II** | **Companies and LLPs** (**corporate debtors**), **personal guarantors** to them, and other bodies the Government notifies |
| **Part III** | **Partnership and proprietorship concerns** and **individuals** |

**The ecosystem**

- **IBBI:** the **regulator** (of **insolvency professionals, agencies, entities and information utilities**).
- **Insolvency professionals:** **IRP, RP, liquidator, bankruptcy trustee**.
- **Information utilities:** hold **financial information** and the **certificate of default**.
- **Financial creditors:** **lent money** (time value). **Operational creditors:** supplied **goods or services on credit**, or took **advances** for them.
- **Committee of creditors (CoC).**
- **Courts:** **NCLT** and **NCLAT** (corporate), **DRT** and **DRAT** (individuals and partnerships), **Supreme Court**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware stresses that the Code is a consolidation, which is why it is called a Code rather than an Act.

items.title: From debtors in possession to creditors in control
items.core_explanation_md:
**Before the Code:** the **debtor stayed in possession** and the creditor chased it through many laws.

**Under the Code:**

1. On **appointment of the IRP**, the **board's powers are suspended** and the IRP takes over as **CEO**.
2. When the **committee of creditors** is formed, it **supersedes the board**.
3. **Original promoters and their related parties** cannot bid for the **corporate debtor** (**section 29A**): ownership, control and management leave the existing promoters.

The courseware calls the Code **debtor-friendly** in one sense: it asks whether the **business can be revived**, treating the **business separately from its promoters**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The pre-pack reverses part of this: the debtor stays in management while a base plan is prepared.

items.title: Starting a corporate insolvency resolution process and the moratorium
items.core_explanation_md:
**Threshold:** the Code applies where the **minimum default is Rs 1 lakh**; the Government may notify a **higher minimum, not above Rs 1 crore** (the courseware gives **Rs 1 crore**).

**Who can apply:** a **financial creditor** (alone or jointly), and, per the courseware, an **operational creditor** or the **corporate debtor**. **Default** means non-payment of **dues in full or part to any creditor**: a third party can start the process even when the bank's account is **standard**.

**Admission:** the Adjudicating Authority admits or rejects a financial creditor's application **within 14 days**, after giving **7 days** to correct defects (2026 amendment).

**Moratorium from the insolvency commencement date prohibits**

1. **Suits and execution** of judgments against the corporate debtor.
2. The corporate debtor **transferring, encumbering or disposing** of assets.
3. **Enforcing security interest**, including under the **SARFAESI Act**.
4. **Recovery of property** by an **owner or lessor**.

**Protected:** supply of **essential goods and services**, and supplies the **RP** treats as **critical** to run the business as a **going concern**.

**IRP:** named by the applicant; **takes over management** and runs the corporate debtor as a **going concern**; for an **operational creditor** application with no proposed IRP, the NCLT appoints one after **consulting IBBI within 14 days**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The moratorium protects assets while the plan is formed; it is why SARFAESI and DRT actions stop.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two actions barred by the moratorium.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Any two of: suits and execution of judgments, disposal of assets by the corporate debtor, enforcement of security interest including SARFAESI action, recovery of property by an owner or lessor.

items.title: The committee of creditors: who is in it and how it votes
items.core_explanation_md:
After **collating claims**, the IRP forms the **committee of creditors (CoC)** of **all financial creditors**.

- A **related party** financial creditor has **no right of representation, participation or voting** (narrow exception for a **regulated** financial creditor that is related **only by debt-to-equity conversion** before commencement).
- **Consortium:** each financial creditor sits with **voting share by the debt owed to it**; with a single **trustee or agent**, each may **authorise the agent, represent itself, appoint an IP, or vote jointly**.
- A **dual creditor** is a financial creditor for its **financial debt** and an operational creditor for its **operational debt**.
- **First meeting** within **7 days** of constitution.

| Decision | Vote of voting share |
| --- | --- |
| Appoint or replace the **resolution professional** | **66 per cent** |
| **Extend** the process beyond 180 days | **66 per cent** |
| **Approve a resolution plan** | **66 per cent** |
| **Decide to liquidate** | **66 per cent** |
| **Withdraw** the application | **90 per cent** |

**Courseware (needs_review):** operational creditors take an **observer** role (voting only where there are **no financial creditors**); **quorum 33 per cent by value**; routine matters **51 per cent**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Because votes are by value of financial debt, large lenders such as banks dominate decisions.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Not less than 66 per cent of the voting share of the financial creditors.

items.title: Who cannot submit a resolution plan: section 29A
items.core_explanation_md:
A person (or anyone **acting jointly or in concert** with them) **cannot submit a plan** if they:

| | Ground |
| --- | --- |
| (a) | Are an **undischarged insolvent** |
| (b) | Are a **wilful defaulter** (RBI guidelines) |
| (c) | Have an **NPA account** (own, or of a corporate debtor they manage or control or promote) for **at least one year** before the CIRP began, **unless all overdue amounts with interest and charges are paid before submitting the plan**; **does not apply** to a **financial entity** that is **not a related party** of the corporate debtor |

items.title: The resolution plan and its approval
items.core_explanation_md:
A **resolution applicant** submits the plan to the **RP** with an **affidavit of eligibility under section 29A**.

**What the plan states (courseware, needs_review):** amounts to **operational and financial creditors**; treatment of **all stakeholders**; **past failures** of the applicant; **term, schedule and management**; how the **cause of default** is addressed; **feasibility and viability**; **approvals** needed; the applicant's **experience and capacity**. It must provide for **insolvency resolution costs** and pay **operational creditors not less than the liquidation value**, ahead of financial creditors.

**Approval**

1. The **RP checks** each plan for compliance.
2. The **CoC** evaluates the plans strictly on the **evaluation matrix**.
3. A plan is approved by **not less than 66 per cent** of the financial creditors' voting share, considering **feasibility and viability**, the **manner of distribution** (which may reflect the **section 53 priority** and the **value of security**).
4. The approved plan goes to the **Adjudicating Authority**.

The applicant may attend CoC meetings as an **observer**.

items.title: The order of priority in liquidation
items.core_explanation_md:
| Rank | Dues paid |
| --- | --- |
| **(a)** | **Insolvency resolution process costs** and **liquidation costs**, in full |
| **(b)** | **Workmen's dues (24 months)** and **debts to a secured creditor who relinquished security** (rank **equally**) |
| **(c)** | **Wages and dues of other employees (12 months)** |
| **(d)** | **Financial debts owed to unsecured creditors** |
| **(e)** | **Dues to Central and State Governments (2 years)** and **secured creditor's unpaid balance after enforcement** (rank **equally**) |
| **(f)** | **Any remaining debts and dues** |
| **(g)** | **Preference shareholders** |
| **(h)** | **Equity shareholders or partners** |

**Rules:** within a rank, **pay in full or pro rata**; **contracts that disturb the order are ignored**; the **liquidator's fee** is deducted **proportionately from each class**.

**Secured creditor's choice**

- **Relinquish** the security to the liquidator and join at rank (b).
- **Stay outside** and enforce the security itself; any **shortfall** ranks at **(e)**; any **surplus** goes to the liquidator.
- **2026 clarification:** if the security relinquished is worth **less than the debt**, the creditor is **secured to the value of the security** and **unsecured for the rest**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The relinquishing secured creditor shares rank (b) with workmen, which is why many banks weigh the choice.

items.title: The pre-packaged insolvency resolution process (PIRP)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Who can use it:** corporate debtors that are **MSMEs**, and other corporate debtors with a section 4 default, subject to conditions.

**Conditions**

- **No PIRP or CIRP in the last three years**; not now in CIRP; no liquidation order; **eligible under section 29A**.
- **Unrelated financial creditors with at least 66 per cent in value** approve **the proposed RP** and the **filing**; the **base resolution plan** is put before them.
- A **majority of directors or partners** declare the filing will be made **within 90 days**, that the process is **not to defraud**, and name the RP.
- **Members pass a special resolution** (or **three-fourths of partners** a resolution) to file.

**Process**

| Step | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Admission | Authority admits or rejects **within 14 days** (7 days to rectify) |
| Whole process | **120 days** from the pre-packaged insolvency commencement date |
| Plan submission | CoC-approved plan to the Authority **within 90 days** |

**Contrast with CIRP (courseware):** PIRP keeps the **debtor in management** with a **base plan** prepared in advance; CIRP puts **creditors in control** from admission; CIRP runs **180 days (extendable to 330)**, PIRP **120 days with no extension**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware's "default up to Rs 1 crore" for PIRP misreads section 4, which only caps the minimum default the Government may notify.
